honorific: Forms of address and self-reference register sheet (zh→en): render royal and imperial first-person pronouns (孤, 朕, 寡人) as natural English 'I' (or majestic 'we' where fitting), never literally as 'lone' or 'the lone one'. Render courtier self-reference 臣 before a sovereign as 'Your servant' or 'Your subject', and sovereign honorifics like 陛下/萬歲 as 'Your Majesty'. Render noble, official, clerical and humble self-references (本王, 下官, 妾身, 贫僧/貧僧, 弟子, 小人, 草民) naturally by speaker role and register, avoiding awkward repetition. Grade forms of address (大人, 殿下, 公子, 先生, 师父/師父, 长老/長老) by speaker-to-listener rank rather than flattening distinct social ranks, and keep one consistent policy for each form of address across the book; never produce ungrammatical calques such as 'the sir'. Avoid stiff Chinese calques: drop demonstrative 'That' before a named character (那<Name> -> '<Name>'), never leak parenthetical glosses into narration, and match singular vs. plural to the characters actually present. Preserve source logic faithfully: negation scope across multi-clause sentences, correlative conditionals (不A，就B = 'if not A, then B'), delayed realizations (良久…才 = 'only after a long while did…'), exact numbers and quantifier polarity (至少 = 'at least'), traditional time units, agent/object direction, and kinship/generational seniority. Resolve idioms (成语) and allusions by their meaning in context rather than translating their surface words literally, and format embedded poems and lyrics with explicit line breaks (\n).
